title: Microbridge prefetch-to-decode playbook (bridgelet)
content:
Goal:
Short, practical playbook for a minimal "bridgelet" layer that mediates prefill -> decode overlap across microbatches and streaming lanes. Focus is on: reducing wasted prefill work, maintaining tail latency for high-priority streams, and making KV residency signals actionable for kernel selection. This doc is exploratory — experimental knobs and rollout plan included.

Context / motivation:
- We already overlap prefill and decode aggressively to improve throughput. But we observe:
  * wasted prefill compute when a stream is prefilled but then re-rolled/backtracked or canceled,
  * priority inversion when long-prefill low-priority jobs block short high-priority decodes,
  * suboptimal kernel choices when KV-residency and token locality aren't communicated to the decode scheduler.
- The "microbridge" (bridgelet) idea: a small, lightweight per-request handoff object that encodes scheduling hints, KV residency metadata, stall budget, and priority tokens. Bridgelets live transiently between prefill and decode and can be coalesced into microbatches for decoding.

Terminology (brief):
- prefill: compute of initial context + KV population and attention states up to first decode token.
- decode: autoregressive token generation loop after prefill.
- bridgelet: ephemeral metadata object created at end-of-prefill describing readiness and constraints for decode.
- stall budget: time a bridgelet can tolerate waiting in the decode queue before being considered expired/cold.
- KV-hit-rate: estimated fraction of KV lookups that will be served from local cache vs remote.

Desired properties:
- Fast path for small, hot streams (short prefix + high kv-hit): low latency, immediate decode scheduling.
- Graceful handling for long-prefill or canceled streams: reclaim prefill resources quickly.
- Fairness across priorities: avoid starvation of high-priority short decodes.
- Kernel affinity: let scheduler pick low-latency vs high-throughput decode kernels using bridgelet signals.

Bridgelet structure (text-only):
- id: opaque request id
- prefetched_tokens: int (prefix length)
- kv_residency_score: float [0.0, 1.0] (estimate of local KV hit rate)
- stall_budget_ms: int (remaining ms before stale)
- priority_tier: string (hi / normal / lo)
- model_variant_hint: string (fp16/q4f16/quant)
- kernel_affinity_hint: string (latency|throughput|mixed)
- parent_shard: id (which GPU pool did prefill run on)
- prefill_epoch: int (monotonic per-server prefill epoch)
- cancel_flag: bool (set by client or orchestrator)

Where the bridgelet lives:
- Stored in an in-memory ring on the GPU-serving host that executed the prefill. Small size (~200–400 bytes). TTL = stall_budget_ms. If microbridge ring fills, oldest bridgelets are expired (and their prefill may be reclaimed).

Handoff flow (end-to-end):
1) Prefill completes -> creates bridgelet and enqueues into local bridge ring + sends pointer to central scheduler.
2) Central scheduler groups bridgelets into microbatches (size <= microbatch_max_tokens, weight by decode cost) while respecting priority lanes.
3) Scheduler picks decode kernel based on aggregated kernel_affinity_hint, kv_residency_score distribution, and tail SLOs.
4) Scheduler issues decode work to a decode worker; worker pulls corresponding KV snapshots/handles from prefill host or shared cache.
5) If bridgelet expires before decode start (stall budget exhausted), the prefill host is signalled to either:
   - checkpoint and keep KV residency (cheap), or
   - evict prefill results to free memory (if memory pressure), or
   - requeue to low-priority bucket for eventual decode (if client still wants result).

Microbatching heuristics:
- Batch should prefer grouping bridgelets with similar kernel_affinity_hint and kv_residency_score to avoid jitter from kernel switching.
- Max microbatch size determined by: GPU token capacity, combined decode token load, and desired latency SLO of highest-priority member.
- When a high-priority bridgelet arrives and no microbatch is imminent, we should preempt an in-flight low-priority microbatch at the software scheduler boundary (not inside GPU kernel). Preemption policy: drain currently running kernel until safe cutpoint, then schedule the high-priority microbatch.

KV residency signal usage:
- kv_residency_score > 0.8: prefer low-latency kernel and place on same-host decode worker to avoid remote KV fetch.
- 0.4 <= kv_residency_score <= 0.8: prefer mixed-kernel that tolerates some remote fetch latency but maintains throughput.
- < 0.4: prefer throughput kernels and consider eager KV prefetch if affordable.

Memory / lifecycle management:
- Prefill memory footprint is tied to bridgelet TTL and expected decode lag. We bound prefill memory by controlling total TTL across active bridgelets (sum of stall_budget_ms * estimated per-token memory).
- Eviction policy: score = A*prefetched_tokens + B*(1 - kv_residency_score) + C*priority_weight - D*recently_accessed. Tune weights A..D in experiments.

Scheduler pseudo-code (simplified):
- on_bridgelet_enqueue(b):
    insert into priority_queues[b.priority_tier] keyed by b.kernel_affinity_hint and kv bucket
    if b.priority_tier == hi: try_immediate_schedule()
    else if enough for microbatch(bucket): schedule_batch(bucket)

- try_immediate_schedule():
    if free_decode_worker with matching kernel_affinity: allocate and run single-bridgelet microbatch
    else if can_preempt_low_priority(): preempt and schedule

- can_preempt_low_priority(): true if high_priority_SLO at risk and preempt cost < SLO_gain

Notes on priority inversion:
- attach an epoch timestamp to every bridgelet and enforce a max wait time that is a function of priority tier.
- implement donation: when a high-priority bridgelet is blocked by older low-priority batches occupying decode slots, temporarily boost priority of low-priority peers to finish sooner when that results in net SLO improvement (heuristic-based).

Kernel selection knobs:
- kernel_affinity_hint (from bridgelet) is advisory; scheduler also considers current GPU temperature, kernel warm caches, and amortized kernel switch cost.
- prefer keeping same kernel across consecutive microbatches if average kv_residency_score variance < threshold.

Experiments to run (A/B plan):
1) Canary bridgelet ring enabled in single region: measure p50/p95 decode latency for hi/normal/lo, wasted prefill token ratio, GPU utilization. (metric window 1s/1m/15m)
2) Vary stall_budget_ms across client classes (50ms, 200ms, 1s) and measure change in prefill eviction rate and cost-per-successful-decode.
3) Test preemption aggressiveness: preempt none / drain / force; measure SLO improvement vs throughput loss.
4) KV affinity experiment: route high kv_residency bridgelets to co-located decoders vs generic pool; measure remote_kv_fetches/sec and p99 tail.

Key metrics to track:
- decode_start_delay_by_priority (histogram)
- wasted_prefill_ratio = tokens_prefetched_but_not_used / tokens_prefetched_total
- gflops_utilization and token/sec per GPU (throughput)
- p50/p95/p99 tail latency broken out by priority tier and by kv_residency_bucket
- prefill_eviction_rate and avg_time_to_eviction
- kernel_switch_rate and amortized_switch_cost_ms

Rollout plan:
- phase 0: local-only prototype on a dev cluster; no client traffic, collect synthetic workload data.
- phase 1: canary region with feature-flag; 5% traffic, aggressive metrics alerts for p95 regressions and wasted_prefill_ratio increase.
- phase 2: opt-in customers (solutions-engineering) with heavy streaming use-cases.
- phase 3: global rollout after tuning.

Operational considerations / failure modes:
- lost bridgelets: if bridge ring is lost (host crash), client should be informed; fallback is to re-run prefill or switch to cold decode (higher latency).
- mis-estimated kv_residency_score: leads to kernel mismatch -> small latency blips. Mitigation: conservatively bias score downward until warmed by online calibration.
- priority amplification via bad clients: enforce per-customer token quotas and rate limiting at API gateway so bridge-level preemption isn't abused.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should bridgelet include a compact signature of the KV keys it touched so remote decoders can do partial warmup? (Privacy / size tradeoff)
- How to merge bridgelets for multi-turn dialogues when later turns alter KV residency semantics?
- Fine-grained eviction scoring weights — run grid search and evaluate cost curve.
- Add simple simulator to validate fairness and throughput tradeoffs before full rollout.

Implementation notes / immediate engineering tasks:
- small in-proc ring buffer on prefill host for bridgelets (C++), with lock-free enqueue/dequeue.
- scheduler extension to accept pointer + cost model, group into microbatches, and expose telemetry.
- add bridgelet-aware kernel selector in runtime (hooks to choose kernel at enqueue time).
- create metrics dashboard (Grafana) for metrics listed above and alert rules (p95 decode latency regressions > 10% baseline).

References and related artifacts:
- jira:RINF-2389 – prefetched state lifecycle
- github PR #412 – initial bridgelet ring prototype
- confluence:serving-runtime/prefill-decode-bridge – prior sketches and measurements

Quick notes to self:
- avoid overfitting to single microbatch size; make batching cost model adaptive.
- focus first on high-priority fast-turn workloads (chat assistants) since user experience impact is large.

If you want, I can: provide a small simulator script (python pseudocode) that exercises eviction/preemption policies and outputs the metrics above, or draft an RFC for rollout with exact experiment thresholds and alert severities.
